triage.name: Metabolic Syndrome
triage.reason: Primary care case: incidental findings of central obesity, hypertension, dysglycemia and dyslipidemia assembled into a diagnosis with management implications.

demographics: Prevalence rises with age and is higher in Mexican American and other Hispanic adults than in White or Black adults in the US
More common in people with lower income and lower education levels
More common in postmenopausal women than in premenopausal women

risk_factors.text: Family history of type 2 diabetes or early heart disease
Diet high in saturated fat, refined carbohydrates and added sugar
Poor sleep or obstructive sleep apnea

family_history: Type 2 diabetes in a parent or sibling
Early coronary artery disease in a first-degree relative
Hypertension or dyslipidemia in a first-degree relative
social_history: Sedentary desk job or little leisure-time exercise
High intake of fast food, sugary drinks or alcohol
Lower household income or food insecurity
Chronic stress or short sleep duration

chief_complaints.text: My doctor says my blood pressure and sugar are up and my cholesterol is bad
I've been putting on weight around my middle
I just feel tired all the time
I have no symptoms — it came up on my routine labs

hpi.onset: Gradual, over years; usually discovered incidentally at a routine visit or when screening labs are checked
hpi.duration: Present for years by the time it is recognized
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive; weight and waist circumference creep up, and blood pressure, glucose and lipids drift upward over time. Many patients remain asymptomatic until a complication such as diabetes or a cardiac event appears.
hpi.location: Central/abdominal weight gain; no focal pain
hpi.quality: Constitutional and metabolic rather than a discrete symptom
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; the condition itself is usually silent, and severity is judged by how many risk factors are present and how abnormal they are
aggravating: Medications that cause weight gain or raise glucose and blood pressure

associated_symptoms.text: Increased waist size or clothes fitting tighter around the middle
Loud snoring or witnessed pauses in breathing during sleep
Exertional shortness of breath with modest activity
Dark, velvety skin folds at the neck or armpits

pertinent_negatives: Chest pain or pressure at rest
Focal weakness, numbness or trouble speaking
Fever, night sweats or drenching sweats
Blood in the stool or black stools
Polyuria with weight loss and blurred vision suggesting uncontrolled diabetes
Heat or cold intolerance with tremor or hair changes

negatives: Pain in the calves when walking
Deepening voice or enlarging hands and feet

positives.text: Witnessed pauses in breathing during sleep
Aching knees or low back pain

negatives: Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour

positives.text: Dark, velvety skin at the neck or armpits

negatives: Numbness or tingling in the feet

atypical.how_it_differs: Metabolic syndrome is increasingly recognized in children and adolescents with obesity, but waist thresholds are age- and sex-specific and the condition is usually found on screening rather than from symptoms.
Sarcopenic obesity can hide a large waist, and frailty, cognitive decline or polypharmacy may dominate the picture; blood pressure and glucose may already be treated, masking the underlying cluster.
missing_classic_features: Untreated high blood pressure or glucose

atypical.how_it_differs: Normal pregnancy raises triglycerides, lowers HDL and increases insulin resistance, so the usual cutoffs do not apply; metabolic syndrome is generally assessed before pregnancy or after delivery.
missing_classic_features: Interpretable lipid and glucose values during pregnancy

atypical.how_it_differs: Patients with established type 2 diabetes almost always meet the glucose criterion, so the diagnosis turns on waist, blood pressure and lipid components, and symptoms may reflect hyperglycemia rather than the syndrome itself.
missing_classic_features: A separate glucose abnormality to uncover

atypical.how_it_differs: Severe obesity can produce the full cluster at a younger age, and the presentation may be dominated by mechanical symptoms such as joint pain, shortness of breath and sleep apnea rather than by abnormal labs.

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable, no distress; central adiposity may be the only obvious feature
general.moderate: Well-appearing but overweight with a prominent abdomen; may be mildly short of breath with exertion during the exam
general.severe: Obese with a protuberant abdomen; may be dyspneic on minimal exertion or when lying flat, and may have lower extremity edema
general.critical: Not a feature of metabolic syndrome itself; an acute complication such as myocardial infarction, stroke or hyperglycemic crisis may dominate the picture

findings.maneuver: Measure the waist circumference at the top of the iliac crests at the end of a normal expiration
findings.finding: Waist circumference 40 inches (102 cm) or more in men, or 35 inches (88 cm) or more in women

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the abdomen with the patient standing and supine
findings.finding: Increased central/abdominal fat with a protuberant, apple-shaped abdomen

findings.maneuver: Measure height and weight and calculate BMI
findings.finding: BMI in the overweight or obese range (25 kg/m2 or higher)

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure in both arms with an appropriately sized cuff after 5 minutes of rest
findings.finding: Blood pressure 130/85 mm Hg or higher

findings.maneuver: Inspect the posterior neck, axillae and skin folds
findings.finding: Dark, velvety, thickened skin (acanthosis nigricans), a marker of insulin resistance

findings.maneuver: Press over the dorsum of each foot and the lower shins
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the lower extremities

findings.maneuver: Inspect the elbows, knees, Achilles tendons and palms
findings.finding: Xanthomas or xanthelasmas suggesting a primary lipid disorder

findings.maneuver: Palpate the thyroid gland and inspect for goiter
findings.finding: No goiter, nodule or thyroid enlargement

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart in the standard four valve areas
findings.finding: Normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs or gallops
Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheezing

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for tenderness, masses and hepatomegaly
findings.finding: Soft, nontender abdomen without organomegaly or mass

findings.maneuver: Test sensation to light touch and pinprick in the feet and check ankle reflexes
findings.finding: Intact sensation and normal reflexes without peripheral neuropathy

labs.caveat: Must be a fasting sample. 100-125 mg/dL is impaired fasting glucose; 126 mg/dL or higher on two occasions meets the glucose criterion and suggests diabetes.
5.7-6.4% is prediabetes; 6.5% or higher meets the glucose criterion and suggests diabetes. Less reliable in anemia, hemoglobinopathy, pregnancy and recent transfusion.
Fasting sample preferred. Values of 500 mg/dL or higher raise the risk of pancreatitis and warrant treatment for that reason alone.
Low HDL is under 40 mg/dL in men and under 50 mg/dL in women; the ranges shown are for men. Low HDL is a criterion only when triglycerides are also elevated or when HDL-lowering treatment is in use.
Not part of the syndrome definition but needed for cardiovascular risk estimation and treatment decisions.
Not a criterion for the syndrome; drives statin decisions and cardiovascular risk scoring.
Mild elevation suggests nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, which commonly accompanies the syndrome. Marked elevation points to another cause.
Usually lower than ALT in fatty liver disease; a ratio above 1 raises concern for alcohol-related or advanced liver disease.
Sensitive but nonspecific marker of fatty liver and alcohol use.
A high-sensitivity assay is used; mild elevation reflects the low-grade inflammation of the syndrome and adds to risk estimates.
Ordered to exclude hypothyroidism as a cause of weight gain, dyslipidemia and fatigue before attributing everything to the syndrome.
Hyperuricemia and gout are common companions of the syndrome; ranges shown are for men.
Proteinuria suggests kidney damage from diabetes or hypertension and should be quantified with a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio.
Negative. Checked in anyone who could be pregnant before starting medications or attributing amenorrhea to polycystic ovary syndrome.

findings.finding: Normal sinus rhythm with no acute ischemic changes
Left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria with secondary repolarization changes
Nonspecific ST-T wave flattening or inversion

imaging.preferred_when: When a carotid bruit is heard or atherosclerotic disease is suspected

findings.text: Intima-media thickening of the carotid arteries
Focal atherosclerotic plaque without hemodynamically significant stenosis

imaging.preferred_when: Persistently elevated aminotransferases or right upper quadrant pain

findings.text: Increased hepatic echogenicity (bright liver) consistent with hepatic steatosis

imaging.preferred_when: Murmur, signs of heart failure, or unexplained dyspnea

findings.text: Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with preserved ejection fraction
Normal chamber sizes and systolic function

imaging.preferred_when: Chest pain with an inconclusive stress test or intermediate pretest probability of coronary disease

findings.text: Coronary artery calcification and nonobstructive plaque

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast

findings.text: Not indicated for the diagnosis of metabolic syndrome; incidental hepatic steatosis or visceral adiposity may be reported

initial.why: Fasting glucose for the glucose criterion, plus kidney function and electrolytes before starting antihypertensives
Triglycerides and HDL are two of the five criteria; also gives LDL for risk estimation
Confirms dysglycemia and identifies prediabetes or diabetes
Liver enzymes screen for nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, a common companion
Excludes hypothyroidism as a cause of weight gain, dyslipidemia and fatigue
Screens for proteinuria and glycosuria from diabetes or hypertension
Hyperuricemia and gout are common in the syndrome
initial.only_if: history of gout or joint symptoms

initial.why: Rules out pregnancy before starting medications

confirmatory.why: Measured at the top of the iliac crests; 40 inches or more in men or 35 inches or more in women is the abdominal obesity criterion
Two readings of 130/85 mm Hg or higher meet the blood pressure criterion
100 mg/dL or higher meets the glucose criterion

supporting.why: High-sensitivity CRP reflects the low-grade inflammation of the syndrome and refines cardiovascular risk
Nonspecific; occasionally checked when an inflammatory cause is being considered
Confirms hepatic steatosis when liver enzymes are elevated

supporting.only_if: carotid bruit or known vascular disease

supporting.why: Assesses left ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic function
supporting.only_if: murmur, heart failure signs or unexplained dyspnea

not_indicated.why: Not part of the evaluation unless anemia or another hematologic problem is suspected
The prothrombotic state is not assessed with routine coagulation tests
Troponin and natriuretic peptides are for acute cardiac presentations, not for diagnosing the syndrome
No role in an asymptomatic metabolic risk cluster

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast
not_indicated.why: Imaging is not needed to diagnose metabolic syndrome
Reserved for symptomatic patients with chest pain, not for routine screening

decision_points: Confirm the waist measurement and blood pressure at a dedicated visit before applying the criteria
Fasting is required for glucose and triglycerides; a nonfasting sample can misclassify the patient
Count the criteria: three or more of the five components establish the diagnosis
Screen for diabetes and fatty liver disease once the syndrome is identified
Pregnancy test before starting medications in anyone who could be pregnant

criteria.name: Metabolic syndrome (ATP III / harmonized criteria)
criteria.summary: The diagnosis requires at least three of five components: abdominal obesity by waist circumference, elevated triglycerides, low HDL cholesterol, elevated blood pressure, and elevated fasting glucose. The harmonized definition uses population-specific waist cutoffs and treats drug treatment for any component as meeting that criterion.
items: Waist circumference 40 inches (102 cm) or more in men, 35 inches (88 cm) or more in women
Triglycerides 150 mg/dL or higher, or on treatment for high triglycerides
HDL cholesterol under 40 mg/dL in men or under 50 mg/dL in women, or on treatment for low HDL
Blood pressure 130/85 mm Hg or higher, or on antihypertensive treatment
Fasting glucose 100 mg/dL or higher, or on treatment for high glucose

differential.name: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
differential.why_considered: Shares central obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia and insulin resistance; many patients with metabolic syndrome already have or will develop diabetes.
differential.trigger: Fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or higher, A1c 6.5% or higher, or symptoms of hyperglycemia

history: Increased thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision or unintentional weight loss
Recurrent infections or slow-healing wounds
Long-standing rather than incidental glucose elevation
exam: Reduced sensation or absent ankle reflexes from peripheral neuropathy
Foot ulcers or calluses
Retinopathy on dilated eye exam
labs: Fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or higher on two occasions, or A1c 6.5% or higher
Random glucose 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Causes weight gain, fatigue, dyslipidemia and mild diastolic hypertension, mimicking the metabolic cluster.
differential.trigger: Fatigue with weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation or a high TSH

history: Cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin and hair thinning
Slowed thinking or depressed mood
Family history of thyroid disease or prior neck radiation
exam: Diffuse goiter or a thyroid nodule
Dry, coarse skin, bradycardia, delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes
Periorbital puffiness
labs: TSH elevated with low free T4
Hypercholesterolemia that improves with thyroid replacement

differential.name: Cushing syndrome
differential.why_considered: Central weight gain, hypertension, hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia closely resemble metabolic syndrome.
differential.trigger: Rapid central weight gain with easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness or violaceous striae

history: Rapid weight gain over months rather than years
Proximal muscle weakness (difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs)
Exogenous steroid use or a history of pituitary or adrenal disease
exam: Violaceous abdominal striae wider than 1 cm
Facial plethora, moon facies, dorsocervical fat pad
Easy bruising and thin skin
labs: Elevated late-night salivary cortisol or 24-hour urine free cortisol
Loss of the normal diurnal cortisol rhythm
Overnight dexamethasone suppression test fails to suppress cortisol
imaging: Pituitary MRI or adrenal CT to localize the source once biochemistry is abnormal

differential.name: Polycystic ovary syndrome
differential.why_considered: Insulin resistance, central obesity, dyslipidemia and irregular menses overlap heavily with metabolic syndrome in women.

history: Oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea since menarche
Hirsutism, acne or male-pattern hair loss
Infertility
exam: Hirsutism (Ferriman-Gallwey scoring), acne, acanthosis nigricans
Enlarged ovaries on pelvic exam
imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound showing multiple small peripheral follicles or increased ovarian volume

differential.name: Familial hypertriglyceridemia
differential.why_considered: Marked hypertriglyceridemia with low HDL can satisfy the lipid criteria without the full metabolic cluster.

history: Strong family history of very high triglycerides or early pancreatitis
Triglycerides elevated since youth, often out of proportion to waist size
Recurrent abdominal pain suggesting pancreatitis
exam: Eruptive xanthomas on the trunk and extremities
Lipemia retinalis on fundoscopy when triglycerides are extremely high
Normal or near-normal waist circumference
labs: Triglycerides often above 500 mg/dL with normal glucose and blood pressure

differential.name: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease
differential.why_considered: Frequently coexists with metabolic syndrome and can be the presenting abnormality when liver enzymes are checked.

history: Often asymptomatic; fatigue or vague right upper quadrant discomfort
Little or no alcohol use
Metabolic risk factors present
exam: Mild hepatomegaly
No stigmata of chronic liver disease unless advanced
labs: Normal platelets and albumin unless cirrhosis has developed
imaging: Right upper quadrant ultrasound showing increased hepatic echogenicity (bright liver)
Transient elastography or MRI-PDFF quantifying steatosis and fibrosis

differential.name: Obstructive sleep apnea
differential.why_considered: Common in central obesity and contributes to hypertension, insulin resistance and daytime fatigue.

history: Loud snoring with witnessed apneas
Daytime sleepiness and morning headaches
Unrefreshing sleep despite adequate hours
exam: Large neck circumference, crowded oropharynx, retrognathia
Elevated blood pressure, sometimes resistant to treatment
labs: Elevated A1c and inflammatory markers reflecting the metabolic burden
imaging: Polysomnography showing an elevated apnea-hypopnea index

differential.name: Medication-induced metabolic changes
differential.why_considered: Atypical antipsychotics, corticosteroids, thiazides and beta-blockers can produce weight gain, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia and hypertension.

history: Temporal relationship between starting a culprit medication and the metabolic changes
Weight gain beginning after the drug was started
Use of olanzapine, clozapine, prednisone, hydrochlorothiazide or atenolol
exam: Weight and waist changes tracking the medication course
Cushingoid features if steroids are the cause
labs: Glucose and lipid abnormalities that improve after stopping or switching the drug
Normal values before the medication was started

severity.mild: One or two components present or borderline; waist circumference just above the cutoff, blood pressure 130-139/85-89 mm Hg, fasting glucose 100-125 mg/dL, triglycerides 150-199 mg/dL, HDL mildly low. No target-organ damage.
severity.moderate: Three or more components clearly present; blood pressure 140-159/90-99 mm Hg, fasting glucose 126-180 mg/dL or A1c 6.5-8.0%, triglycerides 200-499 mg/dL, HDL 25-34 mg/dL in men. Early target-organ changes such as hepatic steatosis or left ventricular hypertrophy may be present.
severity.severe: All five components markedly abnormal; blood pressure 160-179/100-109 mm Hg, fasting glucose 181-300 mg/dL or A1c 8.1-10.0%, triglycerides 500-999 mg/dL, HDL 15-24 mg/dL in men. Established complications such as diabetic kidney disease, diastolic dysfunction or clinical atherosclerotic disease.
severity.critical: Not a feature of metabolic syndrome itself, but a hyperglycemic crisis (diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state), acute coronary syndrome, stroke or severe hypertriglyceridemia with pancreatitis can occur as a consequence and dominate the presentation.

red_flags.finding: Chest pain or pressure at rest, or new exertional chest pain
red_flags.meaning: Possible acute coronary syndrome; needs immediate ECG and troponin

red_flags.finding: Focal weakness, numbness, trouble speaking or sudden vision loss
red_flags.meaning: Possible stroke or transient ischemic attack; urgent imaging and neurology evaluation

red_flags.finding: Blood pressure 180/120 mm Hg or higher with headache, chest pain, visual changes or confusion
red_flags.meaning: Hypertensive emergency; needs immediate treatment and evaluation for end-organ damage

red_flags.finding: Fasting glucose above 300 mg/dL with polyuria, polydipsia, vomiting or altered mental status
red_flags.meaning: Hyperglycemic crisis (DKA or HHS); requires urgent fluids, insulin and electrolytes

red_flags.finding: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with triglycerides above 500 mg/dL
red_flags.meaning: Hypertriglyceridemia-induced acute pancreatitis; needs lipase, imaging and triglyceride-lowering therapy

red_flags.finding: Rapid weight gain with proximal weakness, easy bruising or violaceous striae
red_flags.meaning: Suggests Cushing syndrome rather than primary metabolic syndrome; needs cortisol testing

complications.name: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
clues: Fasting glucose rising above 126 mg/dL or A1c above 6.5%
Increasing thirst, urination or blurred vision

complications.name: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (myocardial infarction, stroke, peripheral arterial disease)
clues: Exertional chest pain or shortness of breath

complications.name: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and steatohepatitis
clues: Right upper quadrant discomfort or hepatomegaly

complications.name: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
clues: Exertional dyspnea and lower extremity edema
Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction on echocardiogram

complications.name: Hypertriglyceridemia-induced acute pancreatitis
clues: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back

complications.name: Gout
clues: Acute monoarticular joint pain, classically the first metatarsophalangeal joint

special_populations.differences: Metabolic syndrome is increasingly recognized in children and adolescents with obesity, but waist thresholds are age- and sex-specific and the diagnosis is usually made on screening rather than from symptoms. Lifestyle intervention is the mainstay; medications are used cautiously.

Sarcopenic obesity can hide a large waist, and frailty, cognitive decline or polypharmacy may dominate the picture. Blood pressure and glucose may already be treated, masking the underlying cluster. Treatment targets are individualized to avoid hypoglycemia and orthostatic hypotension.

Normal pregnancy raises triglycerides, lowers HDL and increases insulin resistance, so the usual cutoffs do not apply. Metabolic syndrome is generally assessed before pregnancy or after delivery. Gestational diabetes and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are more common in women with the syndrome.

Patients with established type 2 diabetes almost always meet the glucose criterion, so the diagnosis turns on waist, blood pressure and lipid components. Management focuses on glycemic control, cardiovascular risk reduction and screening for complications such as nephropathy and retinopathy.

Severe obesity can produce the full cluster at a younger age, and the presentation may be dominated by mechanical symptoms such as joint pain, shortness of breath and sleep apnea rather than by abnormal labs. Weight loss, including metabolic surgery when appropriate, has the largest impact.

Blood pressure targets and medication choices must account for reduced kidney function; metformin is avoided below certain eGFR thresholds, and statins and antihypertensives are dose-adjusted. Proteinuria should be quantified and monitored.

key_questions.question: Have you noticed your weight or waist size changing over the past few years?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual central weight gain; clothes fitting tighter around the middle

key_questions.question: Has anyone ever told you your blood pressure, blood sugar or cholesterol was high?
key_questions.looking_for: Known hypertension, prediabetes, diabetes or dyslipidemia; treatment for any of these counts as meeting that criterion

key_questions.question: What did you eat yesterday, and how often do you eat fast food or drink sugary beverages?
key_questions.looking_for: High intake of saturated fat, refined carbohydrates and added sugar

key_questions.question: How much physical activity do you get in a typical week?
key_questions.looking_for: Little or no leisure-time exercise; sedentary desk job

key_questions.question: Do you snore loudly, or has anyone seen you stop breathing during sleep?
key_questions.looking_for: Obstructive sleep apnea, which contributes to hypertension and insulin resistance

key_questions.question: Do you feel tired or short of breath with activities that used to be easy?
key_questions.looking_for: Fatigue or exertional dyspnea suggesting early cardiac or metabolic complications

key_questions.question: Do you have any dark, velvety patches of skin at your neck or armpits?
key_questions.looking_for: Acanthosis nigricans, a marker of insulin resistance

key_questions.question: Are you taking any medicines for mood, blood pressure or another condition?
key_questions.looking_for: Atypical antipsychotics, corticosteroids, thiazides or beta-blockers that can cause weight gain, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia or hypertension

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol or an early heart attack?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of type 2 diabetes or early coronary artery disease

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or use tobacco?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or former smoking, which adds to cardiovascular risk

key_questions.question: For women: are your periods regular, and have you been told you have polycystic ovary syndrome?
key_questions.looking_for: Oligomenorrhea or PCOS, which is associated with insulin resistance and the metabolic cluster

key_questions.question: Have you had chest pain, weakness on one side, trouble speaking or sudden vision loss?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms of acute coronary syndrome or stroke that require immediate evaluation

reasoning_points: At least three of the five components are present: abdominal obesity by waist circumference, elevated triglycerides, low HDL cholesterol, elevated blood pressure and elevated fasting glucose
Waist circumference is 40 inches (102 cm) or more in men or 35 inches (88 cm) or more in women
Triglycerides are 150 mg/dL or higher, or the patient is on treatment for high triglycerides
HDL cholesterol is under 40 mg/dL in men or under 50 mg/dL in women, or the patient is on treatment for low HDL
Blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg or higher, or the patient is on antihypertensive treatment
Fasting glucose is 100 mg/dL or higher, or the patient is on treatment for high glucose
The presentation is usually incidental and asymptomatic apart from central weight gain
Look-alikes such as hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome and medication effects have been considered and excluded
Cardiovascular risk has been estimated and complications such as diabetes, fatty liver disease and sleep apnea have been screened for

easy: Middle-aged adult with a large waistline and known high blood pressure, high sugar and bad cholesterol
Routine labs show elevated fasting glucose, high triglycerides and low HDL
Central obesity is obvious on exam and the patient reports a sedentary lifestyle
medium: Patient already on treatment for hypertension and dyslipidemia, so the untreated values are masked and the criteria must be counted from the medication history
Waist circumference is borderline and the diagnosis hinges on the lipid and glucose components
Acanthosis nigricans and skin tags point to insulin resistance without florid obesity
hard: Older adult with sarcopenic obesity and a normal-appearing waist but abnormal glucose and lipids
Patient taking olanzapine or prednisone whose metabolic changes are attributed to the medication rather than the syndrome
Woman with polycystic ovary syndrome and irregular periods where the metabolic cluster is overlooked
Patient with established type 2 diabetes where the glucose criterion is already met and the other components must be actively sought
